query: Platinum-group metals can promote distinct reactions, and earlier PGM-based nanoscale catalysts showed strong activity, selectivity, and durability in complex catalysis. A representative catalyst was reported to perform particularly well in ethanol oxidation, which involves 12-electron and 12-proton transfers, but these performance reports did not establish a comprehensive causal explanation of its behavior during operation. Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis explaining what governs its catalytic activity, selectivity, or durability and why. Define an unnamed controlled change with a suitable baseline, the predicted observations, the reaction regime in which the hypothesis should apply or fail, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive falsification outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the catalytic activity and selectivity of Pt-based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles with different compositions and surface structures.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the catalytic activity and selectivity do not improve with the predicted changes in composition and surface structure, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Fuel cells are highly desired devices for advanced portable electronic devices and electrical vehicles as they are promising candidates for providing a sustainable, clean and efficient energy supply. The fuel cell catalyses the reactions between a fuel (methanol, ethanol and molecular hydrogen) at the anode and molecular oxygen at the cathode, converting chemical energy into electrical power via the electrochemical process. Catalysts are the central components of fuel cell technologies and largely dictate their ultimate performance. To date, Pt-based nanomaterials are recognized as the most effective electrocatalysts for both the anodic oxidation reaction and the cathodic oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) in the fuel cells. Currently, the state-of-the-art electrocatalysts are almost exclusively small platinum (Pt) nanoparticles (NPs) supported on carbon black (Pt/C). However, the practical large-scale commercialization of fuel cells is still a challenge because of the high cost, poor reaction kinetics, loss of electrochemical surface area and catalytic activity over long-term duration of commercial Pt catalysts. Through such treatments, the hierarchical Pt-Co NWs were uniformly deposited onto carbon support with slightly composition changes from Pt74.8Co25.2 to Pt75.5Co24.5, while retaining their original nanostructures (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Figs 17 and 18). The limited loss of the Co was mainly caused by the formation of Pt-rich surface after this treatment, as confirmed by XPS characterization (Supplementary Fig. 19). Once the Pt-rich surface is present as a thin shell in a core/shell structure, both its activity and durability can be greatly enhanced as a result of the simultaneous downshift of its d-band centre and surface strain induced in the Pt surface.

SummarySearching for an efficient, durable, and low cost catalyst toward oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) is of paramount importance for the application of fuel cell technology. Herein, PtFeCoNiCu high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (PFCNC-HEA) is reported as electrocatalyst toward ORR. It shows remarkable ORR catalytic mass activity of 1.738 A mg−1Pt at 0.90 V, which is 15.8 times higher than that of the state-of-art commercial Pt/C catalyst. It also exhibits outstanding stability with negligible voltage decay (3 mV) after 10k cycles accelerated durability test. High ORR activity is ascribed to the ligand effect caused by polymetallic elements, the optimization of the surface electronic structure, and the formation of multiple active sites on the surface.
